name: Christ Church, Cheltenham
text: Your train passes near Christ Church in Cheltenham, on the train's {side}, a Gothic Revival church begun in 1837 and consecrated in 1840. Inside hangs a glass cross engraved by the artist Bryant Fedden.

name: Greyfriars, Gloucester
text: Your train passes near the remains of Greyfriars in Gloucester, on the train's {side}, a friary founded about 1231. Around 1518 the Berkeleys of Berkeley Castle paid for its church to be rebuilt.

name: Reading Festival bridge
text: Your train passes near the place where the Reading Festival bridge crosses the Thames, on the train's {side}: a temporary footbridge first built in 2008 and put up each year for festival-goers only.

name: Dilton Marsh station
text: Your train passes Dilton Marsh station, opened as a halt in 1937 with no staff. A sign sent passengers to the seventh house up the hill, where Mrs H. Roberts sold tickets from her home until 1947.

name: St Mary's Church, Old Dilton
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church at Old Dilton, on the train's {side}, built in the 14th century beside the Biss Brook and listed Grade I. It is now cared for by the Churches Conservation Trust.

name: Wilton House
text: Your train passes near Wilton House, on the train's {side}, home of the Earls of Pembroke for more than 400 years. It stands on the site of Wilton Abbey, which Henry VIII gave to William Herbert after the Dissolution.

name: Salisbury Cathedral
text: Your train passes near Salisbury Cathedral, on the train's {side}, built in just 38 years from 1220. Its spire is the tallest in England, and it holds one of the four surviving original copies of Magna Carta.

name: West Dean
text: Your train passes near West Dean, on the train's {side}, a village with the border between Wiltshire and Hampshire running through it. A Roman villa site here lies across the border too.

name: Romsey Abbey
text: Your train passes near Romsey Abbey, on the train's {side}, the church of a Benedictine nunnery until the Dissolution and now the largest parish church in Hampshire. Earl Mountbatten of Burma is buried there.

name: Broadlands
text: Your train passes near Broadlands, on the train's {side}, the country house that was home to Lord Palmerston, the 19th-century prime minister. In 1767 Capability Brown began remaking the house and its garden.

name: King George V Graving Dock
text: Your train passes near the King George V Graving Dock in Southampton, on the train's {side}, opened by King George V and Queen Mary in 1933. It was then the largest dry dock in the world, and stayed so for nearly 30 years.

name: Reading Green Park station
text: Your train passes Reading Green Park station, which opened on May 27th 2023, later than planned because of the Covid-19 pandemic. It serves Reading Football Club's stadium and the Green Park business area.

name: Siege of Reading
text: Your train passes near the centre of Reading, on the train's {side}, which a Parliamentarian army of 19,000 under the Earl of Essex besieged for 11 days in April 1643, until the Royalist garrison gave up the town.

name: Sol Joel Park
text: Your train passes near Sol Joel Park in Earley, on the train's {side}, given to Reading in 1927 by Solomon Joel and opened by the Duke of York, later King George VI.

name: Winnersh Film Studios
text: Your train passes near Winnersh Film Studios, on the train's {side}, one of the new film studios built in the early 2020s as demand for space to make films and television grew.

name: Wokingham Town Hall
text: Your train passes near Wokingham Town Hall, on the train's {side}, built in 1860 in the Market Place on the site of an earlier guildhall.

name: Lucas Hospital
text: Your train passes near the Lucas Hospital, on the train's {side}, almshouses founded in 1663 for 16 elderly men from the parishes around, and listed Grade I.

name: Wellington College
text: Your train passes near Wellington College, on the train's {side}, built as a national monument to the first Duke of Wellington. Queen Victoria laid its foundation stone in 1856 and opened it in 1859.

name: The Concrete Elephant
text: Your train passes near the Concrete Elephant, on the train's {side}, a sculpture by Barbara Jones made for the Lord Mayor's Show in London in 1963, to show off a builder's use of reinforced concrete. It now stands beside the A30 in Camberley.

name: St Michael's Abbey, Farnborough
text: Your train passes near St Michael's Abbey in Farnborough, on the train's {side}, founded by the exiled Empress Eugénie as a memorial to her family. She is buried there beside her husband, Napoleon III, and their son.

name: Farnborough Hill
text: Your train passes near Farnborough Hill, on the train's {side}, a house built for the publisher Thomas Longman and bought in 1880 by the exiled Empress Eugénie of France. It is now a girls' school.

name: St Peter's Church, Ash
text: Your train passes near St Peter's Church in Ash, on the train's {side}, which dates back to the 12th century. Domesday Book records a church here, probably built of wood.

name: Wanborough Roman temple
text: Your train passes near the site of a Romano-Celtic temple at Wanborough, on the train's {side}. It was looted between 1983 and 1985; more than a thousand of its silver coins are now in the British Museum.

name: University of Surrey
text: Your train passes near the University of Surrey, on the train's {side}, which began as the Battersea Polytechnic Institute in London in 1891 and became a university in 1966.

name: Guildford Castle
text: Your train passes near Guildford Castle, on the train's {side}, built soon after the Norman Conquest of 1066. Its keep still stands.

name: Shalford Mill
text: Your train passes near Shalford Mill, on the train's {side}, an 18th-century watermill on the River Tillingbourne. In 1932 it was given to the National Trust thanks to Ferguson's Gang, a group of young women who used made-up names.

name: Chilworth gunpowder mills
text: Your train passes near the ruins of the Chilworth gunpowder mills, on the train's {side}, set up by the East India Company in 1625 beside the Tillingbourne. They supplied gunpowder to the government and closed in 1920.

name: Denbies
text: Your train passes near Denbies, on the train's {side}, an estate bought in 1734 by Jonathan Tyers of Vauxhall Gardens. Much of its south-facing land is now planted with the vines of Denbies Wine Estate.

name: Dorking Cockerel
text: Your train passes near the Dorking Cockerel, on the train's {side}, a large sculpture of 2007 on the Deepdene roundabout. It shows a Dorking chicken, a local breed, complete with the breed's fifth toe.

name: Betchworth Castle
text: Your train passes near the ruins of Betchworth Castle, on the train's {side}, a medieval fortified manor house on a sandstone spur above the River Mole.

name: Reigate Priory
text: Your train passes near Reigate Priory, on the train's {side}, founded in the 1200s as an Augustinian priory. After the Dissolution it became a house; one later owner was Charles Howard, who led the English fleet against the Spanish Armada.

name: Reigate Castle
text: Your train passes near the site of Reigate Castle, on the train's {side}, now a public park. None of the castle buildings survive, but a cave below it, Baron's Cave, is sometimes open for tours.

name: Royal Earlswood Hospital
text: Your train passes near the Royal Earlswood Hospital, on the train's {side}, the first establishment to care specifically for people with learning disabilities. John Langdon Down, after whom Down's syndrome is named, ran it from 1855 to 1868.

name: All Saints' Church, Boyne Hill
text: Your train passes near All Saints' Church at Boyne Hill in Maidenhead, on the train's {side}, completed in 1857 and one of the finest early works of the architect G. E. Street. It is listed Grade I.

name: Cannoncourt Farm Pit
text: Your train passes near Cannoncourt Farm Pit, on the train's {side}, old gravel pits where Stone Age tools were found in the early 1900s, among them the largest hand axe ever found.

name: Bourne End Railway Bridge
text: Your train crosses the River Thames at Bourne End, on a bridge first built in wood by Isambard Kingdom Brunel for the line's opening in 1854 and rebuilt in steel in 1895.

name: Marlow Bridge
text: Your train passes near Marlow Bridge, on the train's {side}, a suspension bridge over the Thames built between 1829 and 1832 by William Tierney Clark, who also designed the Chain Bridge over the Danube in Budapest.

name: Windsor Castle
text: Your train passes near Windsor Castle, on the train's {side}, used by the monarch since the time of Henry I, who reigned from 1100 to 1135: the longest-occupied palace in Europe.

name: Exeter Cathedral
text: Your train passes near Exeter Cathedral, on the train's {side}, complete by about 1400. It has the longest unbroken medieval stone vaulted ceiling in the world.

name: Polsloe Priory
text: Your train passes near what remains of Polsloe Priory, on the train's {side}, a Benedictine nunnery founded around 1159. At the time it was the only religious house for women in Devon.
